measurement.happened:
The dominant story of the week in Indonesia was the signing of a comprehensive trade deal with the European Union after a full decade of negotiations. The EU member-state governments authorised the signature on November 18 (Reuters, Al Jazeera), and the actual signing took place on November 21 (Reuters, Deutsche Welle). The agreement covers everything from palm oil to pharmaceuticals (Deutsche Welle) and is widely framed as a strategic response to the tariff environment created by the United States (Al Jazeera). For a country that has long courted both blocs, locking in a free-trade framework with the EU while simultaneously deepening ties with China gives Prabowo Subianto a broader diplomatic hand to play. The deal is likely to be the single most consequential economic event for Indonesia in years, and it will dominate headlines for weeks as implementation details emerge.

The second major thread was the rupiah crisis. The currency hit record lows against the dollar on November 16 (Bloomberg), and the Bank Indonesia resumed rate hikes on November 18, a move that surprised many analysts (Bloomberg, WSJ, Reuters). The rate decision was described as a close call (Bloomberg), and analysts warned the central bank faces an uphill battle to stem the slide (Bloomberg). The political turmoil, including the wiretapping scandal, was explicitly cited as adding to market anxiety and a potential MSCI reclassification risk (Reuters). The rupiah weakness is not just a macro issue; it raises import costs for fuel, food, and raw materials, which feeds directly into inflation and the cost of living for hundreds of millions of Indonesians.

The wiretapping scandal consumed the political centre of gravity. On November 17, police dismissed at least two senior officials, including a general, over suspicions that the president's communications had been tapped (Reuters, AP). The AFP reported that a protest video was misrepresented online as a build-up of forces at the national police headquarters, showing how quickly the story mutated in the social-media sphere. Deutsche Welle reported that troops were deployed to Jakarta in the wake of the allegations, a significant and somewhat unusual move that signalled the government took the threat seriously. The ex-president's court appearance was falsely linked to the scandal by some outlets (AFP), adding to the noise. The overall picture is one of a president whose own security apparatus may have been listening to him, with the credibility of the police force and the ruling coalition now in question.

On the environmental and regional front, the annual forest-fire haze returned. Prabowo personally apologised to Singapore and Malaysia on November 15 (Reuters, DW, FT, Al Jazeera), but by November 17 he was also shifting blame, telling the press it was not entirely Indonesia's fault (CNN). Deutsche Welle reported on November 20 that the fires were still spewing smog over both neighbours, and a new sanctuary for rescued orangutans was announced (AFP). Indonesian farmers took an unusual and vivid form of protest, cementing their own feet to the ground (DW), underscoring how the fires and the economic squeeze are hitting the rural population hard.

Indonesia's relationship with China moved into a new gear. Prabowo and Xi discussed future cooperation in the South China Sea (Reuters), and the two countries announced four strategic partnerships worth 71.8 billion dollars (Reuters). At the same time, Indonesia is planning tighter control over soybean imports, which are largely US-sourced (Reuters, Bloomberg), a move that will be read in Washington as a subtle signal. The resource-nationalism thread continued: the government said 70 percent of benefits from mines should go to the state (Bloomberg), it revoked a forest permit from billionaire Surya Paloh's associate Tanoto's firm (Bloomberg), and Franky Widjaja resigned as commissioner of a major palm-oil company (Bloomberg). PT Freeport Indonesia priced a 750-million-dollar senior notes offering (FT), showing the mining sector is still raising capital despite the political risk premium.

In the tech and media space, Google removed 19,000 YouTube channels that were identified as pro-government (Bloomberg), and the Indonesian communications ministry asked Google to clarify the removals (Reuters). Separately, the Straits Times reported that Indonesian police had raided the local unit of Nvidia partner Megaspeed in early 2026 at the US request (Reuters), a detail that adds a layer of great-power tech rivalry to an already tense relationship with Washington. Three people were also arrested in a probe into the manipulation of warrant transactions (Reuters), a smaller but notable financial-crime story.

Smaller but newsworthy items included a magnitude 5.9 earthquake on Flores (Reuters), an explosion at an oil refinery that killed one worker (Reuters), a train colliding with a minibus (Al Jazeera), the resumption of macaque exports for animal testing (DW), a daycare principal jailed for five years over child abuse (BBC), and the passage of the long-debated asset-forfeiture law by parliament (Reuters, Bloomberg), which gives the state a new tool to seize assets linked to corruption and other crimes without a full criminal conviction.
measurement.expected:
The EU-Indonesia trade deal will dominate the news cycle for at least another week. Almost certainly there will be follow-up statements from both the Indonesian Ministry of Trade and the European Commission laying out the first implementation steps, tariff-schedule details, and the timeline for parliamentary ratification in Jakarta. The Indonesian parliament will likely schedule a reading or a brief debate on the agreement. Market commentary will focus on which sectors benefit most, and the palm-oil and pharmaceutical industries will see a surge in analyst notes. I am almost certain this will be the top story through November 28.

The rupiah will remain under pressure. Given that the rate hike was a close call and analysts are divided, I judge it probable that the currency will hover near or at fresh lows, with the Bank Indonesia likely to make additional verbal interventions or hint at further tightening. The MSCI reclassification risk mentioned by Reuters will keep foreign-investor attention on Jakarta. If the rupiah breaks another record, expect a second emergency rate hike or a coordinated intervention with the Ministry of Finance. I rate a further rate hike in the next week as possible but not certain; more likely is a week of nervous holding and commentary.

The wiretapping scandal will not be resolved in a single week. I judge it probable that at least one more police official will be dismissed or suspended, and that the parliamentary committee on public security will hold a hearing. Prabowo will likely make a public statement addressing the scandal directly, either in a cabinet meeting or a press conference. The troop deployment in Jakarta will either be quietly withdrawn or become a talking point for opposition parties. I rate a major new twist, such as the discovery that the tapping extended beyond the president to other ministers, as possible but not probable. A full-blown cabinet reshuffle within this single week is unlikely.

The haze will persist through the dry season, and I expect at least one more round of diplomatic friction with Singapore and Malaysia. Prabowo may issue another statement, and the two neighbours may impose temporary travel or health advisories. I rate a fresh apology or a joint ministerial meeting as probable. The farmers' cemented-feet protest is a vivid image that will be picked up by international media, but I do not expect it to grow into a mass movement within a week.

The 71.8-billion-dollar China partnership package will generate a steady drip of follow-up reporting as individual projects are outlined. I expect at least one concrete project announcement, possibly in infrastructure or energy, by the end of the week. The US reaction to the soybean-control plan will be watched closely; I rate a mild diplomatic note from Washington as possible. The South China Sea cooperation language from the Prabowo-Xi meeting will be dissected by regional analysts, but I do not expect a new incident in the waters within this short window.

The asset-forfeiture law, now signed into statute, will begin its implementation phase. I expect the Ministry of Finance and the Attorney General's office to issue technical guidelines, and the business community, particularly conglomerates with complex asset structures, to lobby for transitional provisions. I rate a high-profile first seizure or a test case as unlikely within one week but possible if a pending case is fast-tracked.

The Google/YouTube channel removal will likely prompt a formal written response from Google to the Indonesian ministry, and the communications ministry may hold a press briefing. I rate a regulatory hearing or a draft amendment to the digital-services rules as possible but not certain within this week. The Megaspeed/Nvidia raid story will see further reporting as the Straits Times and local outlets dig into the scope of the US request, but I do not expect a formal diplomatic protest within the week.

Less likely surprises I would keep on the radar: a second major natural disaster (another earthquake or a volcanic eruption) that briefly steals the headline; a sudden foreign-exchange intervention by the central bank that moves the rupiah by more than two percent in a single session; a parliamentary vote or motion of no-confidence triggered by the wiretapping fallout; or a new round of forest-fire smoke that forces schools in Jakarta to close. Each of these is possible but I would not assign them more than a one-in-four chance.

Things I would not bet on in the next week: a full cabinet reshuffle or the resignation of a minister; a new military confrontation in the South China Sea; a second EU-Indonesia summit or a major new trade announcement with the US; a constitutional amendment or a referendum; a major aviation disaster; or the discovery that the wiretapping involved a foreign intelligence agency. These are all within the realm of possibility over a longer horizon, but for a single week I would put them in the unlikely-to-improbable range.

delta.motion: The most striking shift between the two photographs is the replacement of the vice-presidential resignation as the dominant narrative. In the first week, Gibran's departure, the 120-lawmaker impeachment motion, and the December 2 upper-house vote consumed the political frame. By the second week, the VP vacancy has receded into the background; the formal vote is still ahead, but the story has been overtaken by the signing of the EU trade deal, a decade-long negotiation that lands as the single biggest economic headline. The wiretapping scandal, by contrast, accelerated sharply. It moved from 'police say they have enough evidence for treason charges' to two senior officials including a general being dismissed, troops being deployed to Jakarta, and a protest video being misrepresented online as a military build-up at police headquarters. The escalation from legal procedure to personnel purge and security mobilization happened faster than the first photograph suggested. The rupiah crisis deepened: the currency that hit a record low in week one hit a new record low in week two, and the Bank of Indonesia responded with a surprise rate hike on November 18, a move that was not part of the first week's picture at all. The wildfire theme shifted from a domestic climate-and-enforcement story to an international diplomatic one: Prabowo personally apologized to Singapore and Malaysia, then within two days was telling the press the fires were not entirely Indonesia's fault, while smog was still spilling over both neighbors and farmers in the affected regions took to cementing their own feet to the ground in protest. The China relationship grew from a collection of smaller trade items (coal contract disputes, an LNG plant investment) into a full strategic realignment: Prabowo and Xi discussed South China Sea cooperation, and four partnerships worth 71.8 billion dollars were announced. Resource nationalism, which in week one was a presidential order to give the state a bigger share of mining benefits, hardened in week two into a 70-percent state-benefit rule, the revocation of a forest permit linked to billionaire Tanoto, and the resignation of a commissioner at a major palm-oil company. The tech-and-media theme changed shape: week one was about Meta, TikTok, and Google pushing back on AI copyright revisions; week two is about Google removing 19,000 pro-government YouTube channels and police raiding the local unit of Nvidia partner Megaspeed at the US request, a shift from domestic copyright policy to great-power tech rivalry. What vanished or shrank noticeably: the MSCI index changes that were a headline in week one are reduced to a background reclassification risk in week two; the panda bond, the BP petrol-station stake sale, the Norway carbon-offset deal, the Eramet nickel-mine bid, and the September retail-sales figure all disappear from the second photograph. The earthquake that displaced 13,000 people in week one is replaced by a smaller 5.9 on Flores in week two. New items that had no counterpart in the first photograph include the EU trade deal itself, the Bank of Indonesia rate hike, the troop deployment to Jakarta, the asset-forfeiture law passing parliament, the oil-refinery explosion, the train-minibus collision, the resumption of macaque exports for animal testing, and the daycare principal's five-year jail sentence. Overall, the motion is from a week defined by a single political shock (the VP ouster) and a diffuse set of economic and environmental items, to a week defined by a major diplomatic-economic achievement (the EU deal) layered over a deepening security-and-police crisis, a sharper currency emergency, and a more assertive resource-nationalist turn.
delta.wind: On the VP vacancy, the expectation was that the coming week would be 'consumed by behind-the-scenes negotiations' and that the FT's 'open warfare' warning would play out. In reality, the VP story was not the dominant narrative at all; it was overtaken by the EU deal and the wiretapping escalation. The negotiations are presumably still happening behind the scenes before the December 2 vote, but the public and media attention moved elsewhere. The expectation overestimated the VP story's gravitational pull. On the wiretapping case, the forecast said formal indictments or the filing of charges was 'probable' and a bug sweep was 'possible.' What actually happened was more dramatic and faster: two senior officials were dismissed, troops were deployed to Jakarta, and the social-media distortion of a protest video added a new layer of public anxiety. The direction was right, but the speed and the security-apparatus response (troops in the capital) went beyond what was projected. The 'unlikely' category said a full trial or conviction would not happen in a single week, and that held. On wildfires, the expectation was that the government would follow through on revoking land rights for the eight firms and that Gen Z protests would continue. The government did revoke a forest permit from Tanoto's firm, consistent with the prediction. The protests continued in a vivid form (farmers cementing their feet). The new element not in the forecast was the personal diplomatic apology to Singapore and Malaysia followed by a quick blame-shift, which turned the fires into a trilateral diplomatic episode. The orangutan sanctuary announcement matched the expectation that the habitat-loss story would keep drawing attention. On markets and MSCI, the forecast was that the MSCI index changes would be a headline event and the rupiah would stay under pressure. The rupiah did hit new record lows, confirming the pressure, but the MSCI story was demoted to a background risk factor mentioned in passing. The bigger market story became the EU trade deal and the surprise Bank of Indonesia rate hike, neither of which was in the expectations. The 'things I would not bet on' list included a central bank rate cut and noted a hold or hike was more likely; the hike came, so the instinct was correct, but the rate decision was not called out as a likely headline. On tech and AI law, the forecast expected further pushback from Meta, TikTok, and Google over the AI copyright revisions. That specific story did not dominate; instead, the tech news was Google removing 19,000 pro-government YouTube channels and the Megaspeed raid at US request, a shift toward platform governance and great-power rivalry rather than copyright law. The expectation was in the right neighborhood but the wrong specific story. On the earthquake, the forecast expected continued relief for the 13,000 displaced and possibly an aftershock. A new 5.9 on Flores occurred, but it was a separate event, and the original displacement story faded from the headlines. The expectation was reasonable but the earthquake was a minor thread in both weeks. What came that was not expected at all: the EU trade deal signing as the week's dominant story, the Prabowo-Xi South China Sea and $71.8 billion partnership announcement, the troop deployment to Jakarta, the asset-forfeiture law passing, the Google YouTube channel removals, and the Megaspeed raid. The EU deal in particular was a blind spot; it had been in negotiation for a decade, and the timing of the signature (authorized November 18, signed November 21) was not flagged in the first-week analysis. What this says about the expectations: they were too anchored on the political shock (VP resignation) as the organizing principle of the coming week, when in fact the economic-diplomatic track (EU deal, China partnerships) and the security track (troops, dismissals) had their own momentum that the first photograph underweighted. The expectations also treated the MSCI and panda-bond items as headline material when they were really secondary. And they missed the speed at which the wiretapping scandal would move from legal procedure to personnel purge and military posture. The general calibration was directionally sound on the rupiah, the fires, and the tech tension, but the relative weighting of themes was off, and one major event (the EU deal) was entirely absent from the forecast.
delta.driver: The force moving Indonesia from the first photograph to the second is a government under internal political stress using the window of crisis to accelerate two simultaneous projects: consolidating power at home and diversifying its economic partnerships abroad. The wiretapping scandal and the VP ouster have created a credibility gap around the presidency and the police, and the government's response has been to tighten the security perimeter (dismissals, troop deployment) while the political elite jostle for the VP slot and the wiretapping fallout. At the same time, the weak rupiah and the US tariff environment are pushing Jakarta to lock in new trade frameworks before the dollar keeps sliding, which is why the decade-long EU negotiation was brought to a signature in this exact moment and why the China partnerships and South China Sea talks were elevated to a strategic level. Resource nationalism is the connective tissue: the 70-percent state-benefit rule, the Tanoto permit revocation, and the mining-benefits order are all expressions of a government that wants to extract more value from its own ground before foreign partners and domestic elites capture it. The wildfires are the constant physical pressure that keeps public anger high and makes every policy failure more visible, while the EU deal and the China deals are the government's answer to the question 'what do we have to fall back on when the dollar is strong and the US is unpredictable?' In short, the driver is a Prabowo government that is simultaneously defending its own position against internal rivals, defending the currency against external pressure, and repositioning Indonesia's trade architecture to reduce dependence on any single partner, all in the same seven-day window.

crystal.reasoning:
Starting from the present: the EU trade deal signed on November 21 is the single largest economic-diplomatic event for Indonesia in years, and it will dominate the news cycle for at least another week as implementation details, sectoral winners-and-losers, and political reactions unfold. The rupiah hit a new record low and the Bank of Indonesia surprised the market with a rate hike on November 18; the 'close call' language and the 'uphill battle' framing from analysts tell me the currency fight is far from over. The wiretapping scandal has accelerated from legal procedure to a personnel purge (two senior officials dismissed, a general among them) and a visible security mobilization (troops in Jakarta), with the social-media distortion of a protest video adding a new layer of public anxiety. The wildfires are still spilling smog into Singapore and Malaysia, and Prabowo's apology-then-blame-shift has turned the fires into a trilateral diplomatic irritant. The China relationship has been elevated to a strategic level with the $71.8 billion partnership package and South China Sea cooperation talks. Resource nationalism has hardened into concrete enforcement: the 70-percent state-benefit rule, the Tanoto permit revocation, the Franky Widjaja resignation. The tech story has shifted from domestic copyright law to great-power rivalry: Google removing 19,000 pro-government YouTube channels and the Megaspeed raid at US request. The asset-forfeiture law has passed parliament, giving the state a new extraction tool. Smaller items include the Flores earthquake, the refinery explosion, and the macaque-export controversy.

Extending each theme along its motion: The EU deal was a complete blind spot in last week's forecast, which tells me I underweight 'long-coming' events that suddenly land. The motion shows the economic-diplomatic track (EU, China) and the security track (troops, dismissals) have their own momentum independent of the VP storyline, which has receded. The wiretapping purge accelerated faster than projected, suggesting the next week may see the tail of the purge (one or two more names) rather than a full escalation to trial. The rupiah trajectory is structural, not episodic: one rate hike does not fix a currency that is being sold on governance-risk and US-tariff fears. The fires follow the dry-season calendar and will persist until rains, so the diplomatic friction with Singapore and Malaysia is a multi-week story, not a single-week event. The China partnership is at the announcement stage; the next week will bring the first implementation details and the US trade press will pick up the soybean-import tightening as a signal. The YouTube removal of 19,000 pro-government channels is a blow to the ruling coalition's digital media apparatus and will generate internal political friction as well as a public response from the communications ministry.

Correcting for the wind: Last week's forecast over-anchored on the VP resignation as the organizing principle and underweighted the economic-diplomatic and security tracks. It also overestimated the MSCI story as a headline when it was really a background risk factor. The calibration lesson is: (1) do not let a single political shock define the week when multiple tracks are running in parallel; (2) expect Indonesian political escalation to be faster than Western institutional norms suggest; (3) weight the 'strategic response to US tariffs' framing as an invitation for Washington to react; (4) treat the EU deal not as a one-day signing event but as a multi-week implementation and political-digestion process; (5) the troop deployment and personnel purge are near their peak intensity, so the next week is more likely to show consolidation (statements, confirmations, quiet withdrawals) than a dramatic new escalation, though one more dismissal is plausible. The asset-forfeiture law passing is a new tool that the government will want to use quickly to demonstrate results, so I expect at least one high-profile asset seizure or freeze to be announced. The Google YouTube removal is a story that will generate a government response within days, possibly a new media-regulation signal or a data-localization demand.

What I would not bet on: a full cabinet reshuffle in a single week; the VP being formally appointed (the December 2 upper-house vote is still ahead and the negotiations are behind the scenes); a major new US-Indonesia diplomatic incident (the EU deal is the headline, not a confrontation); a full trial or conviction in the wiretapping case; a sudden rupiah stabilization (the structural drivers are not fixed by one rate hike); the fires being completely extinguished; a new major natural disaster of the scale of the earlier 13,000-displaced earthquake.

WILDFIRES AND REGIONAL DIPLOMACY: The dry season is not over, and the fires are still spilling smog into Singapore and Malaysia. I expect another round of diplomatic exchanges, possibly a joint statement or a follow-up to the apology, and the farmer protests (cementing feet and similar vivid actions) will continue as the rural population bears the brunt. The orangutan sanctuary announcement will be used as a PR counterweight. Singapore and Malaysian media will keep quoting the 'not entirely our fault' line. Direction: persistent haze, continued diplomatic friction, rural protests. Confidence: high on the fires continuing, medium on a new diplomatic incident.

CHINA PARTNERSHIP AND SOYBEAN SIGNAL: The $71.8 billion package of four strategic partnerships and the South China Sea cooperation talks are at the announcement stage. The next week will bring the first implementation details, possibly a specific project launch or a follow-up technical meeting. The soybean-import tightening, which targets largely US-sourced beans, will be picked up by the US agricultural and trade press as a subtle signal of Indonesia's pivot. I would not expect a dramatic US reaction in a single week, but the story will be part of the broader 'Indonesia diversifying away from US dependence' narrative. Direction: continued positive coverage of the China partnership, the soybean story gaining traction in US media. Confidence: medium-high.

RESOURCE NATIONALISM AND CORPORATE ENFORCEMENT: The 70-percent state-benefit rule, the Tanoto permit revocation, and the Franky Widjaja resignation are the latest expressions of a government that wants to extract more value from its own ground. I expect at least one more corporate or permit action in the coming week, possibly another resignation or a new enforcement step in the mining sector. The PT Freeport $750 million bond offering shows the sector is still raising capital, but the political risk premium is rising. The asset-forfeiture law gives the state a new tool, and I expect it to be used in at least one visible case. Direction: continued enforcement, corporate reactions, the 'Indonesia taking back its resources' narrative staying alive. Confidence: medium.

TECH, MEDIA, AND GREAT-POWER RIVALRY: Google's removal of 19,000 pro-government YouTube channels is a significant blow to the ruling coalition's digital media apparatus. The communications ministry has asked for clarification, and I expect a formal government response within days, possibly a new media-regulation signal or a data-localization demand. The Megaspeed raid at US request adds a great-power tech-rivalry layer. The ruling coalition's internal media operation will be in disarray, and the opposition will use the removals as evidence of government overreach. Direction: political friction over the YouTube removals, the tech-great-power angle continuing. Confidence: medium-high on the YouTube story generating a government response.

SMALLER ITEMS: The Flores earthquake relief will continue but will not be a national headline. The oil-refinery explosion investigation will produce preliminary findings. The macaque-export controversy will generate animal-rights debate. The train-minibus collision will be a local story. None of these will displace the larger themes.
crystal.headline: EU Pact Signed as Rupiah Crumbles and Wiretapping Scandal Deepens
emoji_reasons: The EU trade deal, signed after a decade of negotiations, is the single most consequential event of the week and will dominate headlines as implementation details and political reactions unfold.
The rupiah hit a new record low and the Bank of Indonesia was forced into a surprise rate hike, with the currency fight far from over and inflation ticking up.

crystal.tldr: Indonesia's week will be defined by the EU trade deal's aftermath, a rupiah that keeps sliding despite a surprise rate hike, and the wiretapping scandal entering its consolidation phase. The China partnership and resource-nationalism enforcement will keep generating headlines, while the wildfire haze continues to strain relations with Singapore and Malaysia. The VP vacancy negotiations continue quietly behind the scenes ahead of the December 2 vote.
crystal.eli5:
Indonesia just signed a really big trade deal with Europe after ten years of talking. It covers things like palm oil and medicines, and the government is very proud of it. But signing is only the first step. Next week, everyone will be arguing about who wins and who loses, and the United States will be watching closely because Indonesia is doing this partly to show it does not need to depend on America.

At the same time, the Indonesian money (the rupiah) is getting weaker and weaker against the dollar. The central bank had to raise interest rates in a hurry, which is like turning up the price of borrowing money to try to stop people from selling the rupiah. It helped a little, but experts say the fight is not over. If the rupiah keeps falling, things people buy from other countries, like fuel and food, get more expensive, and that makes life harder for regular families.

There is also a big scandal. It turns out the president's own security team may have been secretly listening to his phone calls. Two senior police officials, including a general, got fired over it, and the government sent soldiers into the capital city, which is a big deal. The story is probably near its peak now, but there may be a few more people named or charged. Meanwhile, the vice-president's seat is still empty, and the politicians are quietly figuring out who gets it before a vote in early December.

The forest fires in Borneo are still going, and the smog is still drifting over into Singapore and Malaysia. The president apologized to his neighbors, then quickly said it was not all Indonesia's fault, which did not go down well. Farmers in the affected areas are getting creative with their protests, like cementing their own feet to the ground to show they are stuck and frustrated. The dry season is not over, so the fires are not going to stop on their own.

A few other things are happening too. Indonesia announced a huge package of partnerships with China worth over seventy billion dollars, which is a big strategic move. The government is also cracking down on big companies in the mining and palm-oil sectors, taking a bigger share of the profits for the state. And Google deleted nineteen thousand YouTube channels that were friendly to the government, which is making the ruling party very angry.
